To fix Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 167 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 2 codebook/README/label sources and 167 data columns across 4 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 5 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 3 code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 12 code files.

Spreadsheet Formatting

We examined 3 spreadsheet files in the repository; 1 has at least one formatting issue.

File Sheet Issue Detail
Ratings.xlsx NA Not a rectangular dataset This file reads as a table but is not a usable dataset (86% of columns are free text, not variables). Store the data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook.
Ratings.xlsx Sheet1 Merged cells 11 merged ranges (J1:J2, O1:O2, R1:R2, T1:T2, U1:U2) break the rectangular grid.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

6 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

Respondent Blocks flagged Scales Longest run Short-scale only
SCP-16_0040 46 tfetfeq.q..tfeq.q (1-4, 18 items) same answer 18 times in a row, out of 18 items (flagged at 15) no
SCP-36_0009 46 tfetfeq.q..tfeq.q (1-4, 18 items) same answer 18 times in a row, out of 18 items (flagged at 15) no
SCP-12_0052 46 tfetfeq.q..tfeq.q (1-4, 18 items) same answer 17 times in a row, out of 18 items (flagged at 15) no
SCP-12_0080 46 tfetfeq.q..tfeq.q (1-4, 18 items) same answer 17 times in a row, out of 18 items (flagged at 15) no
SCP-23_0014 46 tfetfeq.q..tfeq.q (1-4, 18 items) same answer 17 times in a row, out of 18 items (flagged at 15) no
SCP-35_0093 46 tfetfeq.q..tfeq.q (1-4, 18 items) same answer 17 times in a row, out of 18 items (flagged at 15) no

What this does not cover. Only 1 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script needs a file that another script should have made.

  • loo_compare_report.R needs phase2_waic_loo.rds, which phase2_waic_loo.R makes.

The other script stopped before it made the file, so fix that script first; this one may then run as well. To make the order clear to readers, number your scripts in the order they run (01_clean.R, 02_model.R), or add one main script that runs the others in order.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • recover_M2.R reads fullfit_M2.rds.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A file may have been renamed.

  • fit_full_M1.R reads nutrient_info_updated.csv; your deposit holds nutrient_info.csv.
  • M1.R reads nutrient_info_updated.csv; your deposit holds nutrient_info.csv.
  • fit_full_M2.R reads nutrient_info_updated.csv; your deposit holds nutrient_info.csv.

  • recover_M2.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.

26 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: mTURK_July2025.csv to mTurk_July2025.csv (in mTurk_analyses.Rmd); mTURK_July2025.csv to mTurk_July2025.csv (in mTurk_analyses_supplement.Rmd); ~/Documents/Github/mTurk_July2025.csv to mTurk_July2025.csv (in M1.R); ~/Documents/Github/src/cleanup.R to cleanup.R (in M1.R); ~/Documents/Github/mTurk_July2025.csv to mTurk_July2025.csv (in M2.R); ~/Documents/Github/src/cleanup.R to cleanup.R (in M2.R); ~/Documents/Github/mTurk_July2025.csv to mTurk_July2025.csv (in M3.R); ~/Documents/Github/src/cleanup.R to cleanup.R (in M3.R); ~/Documents/Github/mTurk_July2025.csv to mTurk_July2025.csv (in M4.R); ~/Documents/Github/src/cleanup.R to cleanup.R (in M4.R), and 16 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. 7 data paths were built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

2 file names in the code are not the same as in the deposit, in case, spaces or punctuation, and exactly one file in the deposit fits. To run the code we corrected this in a copy of the script so that it finds the file. The script itself should be changed, because as written it does not find the file on every system.

File Name in the code Name in the deposit
mTurk_analyses.Rmd mTURK_July2025.csv mTurk_July2025.csv
mTurk_analyses_supplement.Rmd mTURK_July2025.csv mTurk_July2025.csv

Missing inputs

1 input file the code reads is in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.

File Status Reason
nutrient_info_updated.csv absent referenced file is not present in the repository, but a similarly-named file exists: nutrient_info.csv

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 3 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: recover_m2_params_withid.csv, summary_3fac_params.csv, july_3fac_params_recovery.csv.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 18 scripts: 0 ran without error, 17 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

setwd() in the code

3 scripts call setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

File setwd() removed Path(s) it set
loo_compare_report.R 1 /home/processor/Documents/Github
phase2_waic_loo.R 1 /home/processor/Documents/Github
recover_M2.R 1 /home/processor/Documents/Github

Calls that install packages in the code

12 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

Run by another script

1 script is run by another script with source(), so it was not run on its own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on its own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Its outcome is part of the sourcing script’s outcome.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Participants were 1052 adults residing in the United States who completed an online Amazon Mechanical Turk study.

Food rating and choice tasks (Figure 1) Participants completed a food rating task in which they rated 46 food items along 17 separate attributes: protein content, fat content, carbohydrate content, vitamin content, sodium content, sugar content, gluten content, caloric content, healthiness, tastiness, how tasty others think the food is, fillingness, savoriness, pleasantness of texture, disgustingness, feelings resulting from the food, and familiarity.

Next, participants completed a food choice task.

In this task, participants were instructed to choose what they would prefer to eat “right now,” between a reference food (an item the participant had rated neutrally for tastiness and healthiness) and each of the other 45 foods in their stimulus set.

Participants completed the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire-Revised 18; the Cognitive Restraint subscale assessed restrained eating behavior.

“Self-control” can occur on trials in which there is a conflict between choice options, defined as trials on which participants had to choose between a reference item and a food that was either healthy and not tasty or a food that was tasty and not healthy.

Influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors on food choice across individual characteristics Participants were broadly representative of the United States population in terms of individual characteristics, though more highly educated (Lloyd et al; 2020).

Approximately half (51.0%) of participants were female, and the majority (60.2%) aged between 26 and 40 years.

Participants were significantly more likely to choose more savory rather than sweeter foods, consistent with studies showing that protein content is associated with food preferences in humans (32, 33).

Each participant provided a total of 782 ratings (17 ratings for each of the foods in their 46-item set).

Choice Task After all ratings had been provided, participants were instructed to choose what they would prefer to eat “right now,” between a reference food (randomly selected from items the participant had rated neutrally on both the tastiness and healthiness scale) and each of the other 45 foods in their specific stimulus set.

When making their food choices, participants were asked to imagine snack-sized portions of the presented foods.

Self-control “Self-control” can occur on trials in which there is a conflict between choice options, defined as those trials on which participants had to choose between a reference item and a food that was either healthy and not tasty (Healthiness rating above that of the reference item, and Tastiness rating below that of the reference item) or a food that was tasty and not healthy (Tastiness rating above that of the reference item, and Healthiness rating below that of the reference item).

Participants were individuals who completed an online Amazon Mechanical Turk study between July 2018 and August 2019 1, recruited using a convenience sampling strategy, and paid $7.25 for study completion.

Participants provided informed consent by clicking an icon to continue with the experiment.

Participants completed ratings of images of food on 17 different attributes, prior to completing a Food Choice phase in which they indicated whether they preferred a food that varied, displayed on the right, or a constant Reference food, displayed on the left.

Ethics approval statement:

The study was approved by the Columbia University Institutional Review Board.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
