How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Daily food decisions accumulate to impact physical health, but making choices consistent with longer-term health goals can prove challenging. Prior research has focused predominantly on dampening preferences for highly palatable foods, or exerting self-control, as the mechanism for healthier food choices. Consequently, the range of cognitive strategies for healthy eating, and how they vary with demographic characteristics, remains unclear. Here, a large US sample (N = 1,052) completed an online food rating and choice task, and demographic and eating behavior questionnaires. Participants rated foods across 17 dimensions, which were reduced to three underlying core food attributes by factor analysis: Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami (capturing food savoriness). All attributes influenced food choices. A multi-attribute drift diffusion model quantified distinct yet latent choice processes, including the deliberation required prior to making a choice. The influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami on choice varied across the study population. Women, individuals endorsing higher levels of eating restraint, and individuals with lower BMI selected subjectively healthier foods more frequently. Making subjectively healthier choices was not dependent only on engaging self-control. Rather, individuals making subjectively healthier choices perceived subjectively healthier foods as tastier. In addition, individuals endorsing high levels of eating restraint required less deliberation when making choices, suggesting more automatic decision-making. These findings suggest multiple routes to making healthier food choices and question the narrative that food tastiness must be sacrificed to support physical health.

Introduction

Decisions about what to eat are made multiple times a day, every day. The accumulated effect of these decisions impacts health and well-being in the short and long term. Making choices consistent with longer-term health goals is challenging, yet poor diet and (failed) attempts to change diet impose a significant physical and mental health burden for individuals and society (e.g., obesity, cardiovascular disease; (1, 2)). Understanding of the processes guiding food choice is needed for the development of interventions to improve dietary decision making. Some research has described differences in eating patterns among different demographic groups (3), but little is known about the cognitive processes that underlie individual variation in food choices. Here, we characterized how valuation and choice construction processes vary across a large, broadly representative, cohort in the United States (4), with particular focus on factors known to influence dietary decisions: age, gender, BMI, and cognitive restraint around eating (5) (6) (7) (8) (9) (10).

The determinants of eating behavior are complex. The neural mechanisms that regulate homeostatic energy intake have been well characterized (11, 12). However, food intake is not guided by energy needs alone. Cognitive and computational neuroscience studies have yielded a framework for understanding multi-attribute decision-making (13) (14) (15). Within this framework, food choices have largely been examined as the consequence of subjective perceptions of how tasty and healthy food items are. Brain imaging and behavioral data suggest that food options are evaluated along these dimensions prior to combining evaluations into a weighted sum (16) (17) (18), and that the weight applied to a given dimension varies according to individual motivations, values, and states (17, 19).

Tastiness and healthiness attributes are generally considered orthogonal and potentially in conflict (16, 17, 19, 20), and subjective tastiness generally exerts a greater influence on food choice (16, (21) (22) (23) (24). Therefore, the selection of subjectively healthier foods is thought to depend on the exertion of effortful self-control, with studies focusing on the ability to suppress the influence of tastiness (16), to boost the influence of subjective healthiness on choice (17, 25), and approaches to changing the balance between the two influences (17, 26, 27). However, subjective healthiness and tastiness need not be in conflict. Challenging the notion that subjectively healthier choices are made only when self-control is implemented, some individuals (e.g., individuals with the eating disorder, anorexia nervosa, or those endorsing high levels of cognitive restraint around eating) find subjectively healthier items tastier, reducing the need for self-control in those choices (5, (21) (22) (23) 28).

Current understanding of food decisions is also limited by the fact that prior research has focused on the healthiness-tastiness dichotomy, to the exclusion of other attributes that may contribute to the choice process. We previously found that, in addition to subjective healthiness and tastiness factors, foods varied along a dimension that captured protein content, sodium content, low sugar content, and savoriness (henceforth labelled Umami; (4)). Studies with animal models indicate that protein appetite drives behavior and is associated with selective reward responses (29) (30) (31). A few studies in humans have shown that protein content is associated with food choices (32, 33) and that individuals differ in their liking for sweet versus savory foods (34) (35) (36). How the Umami dimension influences choice in the context of the more commonly studied subjective tastiness and healthiness attributes remains unclear.

Here we examined how subjectively healthy food choices are made, which strategies or combination of strategies are implemented, and by whom. We characterized the role of Umami as well as Tastiness and Healthiness factors in food choice, examined multiple decision strategies that may promote subjectively healthier choices, and characterized individual differences in food choice (Fig. 1). For more granular insight into how food choices are made, we applied computational models (drift diffusion models; DDMs) to choice and rating data to separate and quantify distinct choice processes (e.g., choice caution vs. speed of evidence accumulation for separate attributes). Analyses revealed that there were multiple paths to making subjectively healthy choices, and that their use varied with individual characteristics (age, gender, BMI, self-reported cognitive eating restraint). These results have implications for targeted health interventions.

Materials and Methods

The study was approved by the Columbia University Institutional Review Board.

Participants

Participants were 1052 adults residing in the United States who completed an online Amazon Mechanical Turk study.

Food rating and choice tasks (Figure 1) Participants completed a food rating task in which they rated 46 food items along 17 separate attributes: protein content, fat content, carbohydrate content, vitamin content, sodium content, sugar content, gluten content, caloric content, healthiness, tastiness, how tasty others think the food is, fillingness, savoriness, pleasantness of texture, disgustingness, feelings resulting from the food, and familiarity. Next, participants completed a food choice task. In this task, participants were instructed to choose what they would prefer to eat "right now," between a reference food (an item the participant had rated neutrally for tastiness and healthiness) and each of the other 45 foods in their stimulus set.

Questionnaires

Participants completed the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire-Revised 18; the Cognitive Restraint subscale assessed restrained eating behavior. Participants' age, gender, height, and weight were obtained by questionnaire. to completing a Food Choice phase in which they indicated whether they preferred a food that varied, displayed on the right, or a constant Reference food, displayed on the left. The Reference food was selected per individual to be neutral per their ratings of Tastiness and Healthiness. A factor analysis of ratings yielded three central dimensions, subsequently used to examine food choices and their variation with individual characteristics. The Tastiness factor captured texture and familiarity, in addition to how tasty a food was rated. The Healthiness factor captured ratings across various macronutrients in addition to caloric content. The Umami factor captured a savory/sweet dimension including protein and how filling a food was reported to be.

Data analysis

Analyses were completed in R. For all analysis code, see: https://github.com/CaitlinLloyd/ThoughtForFood.

As described previously (4), an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) applied to the rating data indicated that the 17 ratings were best captured by three factors: a Tastiness factor, a Healthiness factor, and an Umami factor capturing a savory/sweet dimension. Capitalization of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami will be used to indicate referral to the composite variable. Logistic mixed effects regression estimated the main effects of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors on choice. Logistic mixed effects regression examined the interaction between the influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors and individual characteristics of interest (Age, BMI, Gender, Cognitive Restraint). Mixed effects regression also estimated the main effects of Healthiness and Umami on Tastiness across all participants, and interactions between individual characteristics and the influence of Healthiness and Umami on Tastiness ratings.

The proportion of subjectively healthy choices was calculated as the proportion of trials in which the participant selected the item rated as healthier; multiple linear regression estimated the association with each individual characteristic of interest.

"Self-control" can occur on trials in which there is a conflict between choice options, defined as trials on which participants had to choose between a reference item and a food that was either healthy and not tasty or a food that was tasty and not healthy. Successful self-control trials were defined as conflict trials in which participants selected the healthy and not-tasty food or did not select the tasty and not-healthy food. Self-control success was calculated for each participant by dividing the total number of successful self-control trials by the total number of conflict trials; multiple linear regression estimated the association with individual characteristics of interest (covarying for total number of conflict trials). To assess whether the use of self-control may be less effortful for certain individuals, mixed effects linear regression was used to estimate the difference in response time between successful and unsuccessful self-control trials.

To examine how subjectively healthy choices related to self-control and Healthiness-Tastiness alignment, the proportion of subjectively healthy choices was regressed onto self-control success and Healthiness-Tastiness alignment (extracted from the model estimating the Influence of Healthiness and Umami on Tastiness, described above).

To further elucidate the cognitive mechanisms underlying food choices, several variants of the multi-attribute drift diffusion model (DDM) were implemented (25, 27, 53, 54; Figure 2). The simplest model had five free parameters: starting bias (initial preference for eating the alternate item); non-decision time (NDT; part of trial in which the decision maker is not actively making a decision; includes time spent encoding choice options and making a motor response); decision boundary separation (bound sep; the amount of evidence required for a decision to be made); drift-rate for Healthiness (extent Healthiness influences choice; dH); and drift-rate for Tastiness (extent Tastiness influences choice; dT). The basic model assumes individuals start to consider information about Tastiness and Healthiness of a given food choice at the same time (non-timevarying DDM). We also considered time-varying DDMs that allow attributes to enter the choice process at different times (25, 27, 55), and those that included the accumulation of evidence for the Umami factor (Umami drift rate; dU). between the reference item-here trail mix, healthier but less tasty than the alternate item of donuts-and the alternate item. In both cases, a relative value signal (RVS) begins with a value set by the bias (for alternate item) parameter (non-zero in these examples) and evolves with Gaussian noise, e, at every timepoint t (shown in segment and equation "A"). Once the Tastiness and Umami latency is reached (blue dotted line), the relative Tastiness and Umami values (difference in Tastiness and Umami between alternate and reference item), ΔT and ΔU, begin contributing to the RVS at a rate determined by its drift slopes dT (drift rate for Tastiness) and dU (drift rate for Umami). This is depicted in segment and equation "B". After the Healthiness attribute latency is reached (green dotted line), the relative Healthiness value (i.e., difference in Healthiness between alternate and reference item) ΔH, begins contributing to the RVS at a rate determined by its drift slope dH (drift rate for Healthiness). This is depicted in segment and equation "C". A decision is reached when the RVS becomes equal to or greater than the threshold for the reference or alternate items. For Decision Maker 1, Healthiness enters the decision process at a similar time to Tastiness and Umami, which leads to an early contribution of the Healthiness attribute to the RVS, and selection of the subjectively healthy choice. For Decision Maker 2, all parameters are the same except that the Healthiness attribute has a larger temporal delay (latency) in its effect on the drift rate. Due to a later entry of Healthiness to the decision process, it begins contributing to the RVS later, and the alternate option boundary (for the tastier donuts) is crossed before the Healthiness attribute has a significant influence on choice. Figure adapted from (27).

Model fit was compared between models using five-fold cross-validation. The model with highest accuracy was considered the best-fitting; relationships between parameters of this model and individual characteristics of interest were examined. Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (56) was implemented as a secondary means of model comparison.

Results

Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors influence food choice The three independent food attribute factors, Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami all influenced food choice (Fig. 3). Individuals were more likely to choose foods that were higher in Tastiness (B = 2.60, 95% CI: [2.50, 2.70], p < 0.001), lower in Healthiness (B = -0.14, 95% CI: [-0.20, -0.09], p < 0.001), and higher in Umami (B = 0.39, 95% CI: [0.34, 0.44], p < 0.001). The quadratic Umami term did not explain additional variance in choice (B = -0.001, 95% CI: [-0.04, 0.04], p = 0.975). Tastiness had the strongest influence on choice, which was also reflected in significant speed-up for choices in which the selected food was higher in Tastiness (B = -27.29, 95% CI: [-36.51, -18.26], p < 0.001; See Supplementary Table S3). Influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors on food choice across individual characteristics Participants were broadly representative of the United States population in terms of individual characteristics, though more highly educated (Lloyd et al; 2020). The characteristics of interest (i.e., age, gender, BMI, Cognitive Restraint) covaried, but associations were small (see Supplementary Table S1 for full details). Approximately half (51.0%) of participants were female, and the majority (60.2%) aged between 26 and 40 years. Mean BMI was 28.43 (SD = 7.11) and mean cognitive restraint score was 46.23 (SD=22.23); see Fig. 4 for distributions of demographic variables. Influence of subjective Tastiness on choice (Figure 5) Tastiness influenced choices more among women (Gender x Tastiness: B = 0.18, 95% CI: [0.09,0.28], p < 0.001), older individuals (B = 0.28, 95% CI: [0.18, 0.37], p < 0.001), and those with lower Cognitive Restraint (Cognitive Restraint x Tastiness: B = -0.29, 95% CI: [-0.39, -0.20], p < 0.001). Additionally, there was an interaction between BMI and Cognitive Restraint: Tastiness influenced choice less among individuals with higher (versus lower) Cognitive Restraint but this effect was greater among those with higher, compared to lower, BMI (BMI x Restraint x Tastiness: B = 0.13, 95% CI: [0.04, 0.22], p = 0.003; Fig 6). Influence of subjective Healthiness on choice (Figure 5) The influence of the Healthiness factor increased with age (Age x Healthiness: B = 0.12, [95% CI: 0.07, 0.17], p < 0.001) and among those reporting higher Cognitive Restraint (Cognitive Restraint x Healthiness: B = 0.12, [95% CI: 0.08, 0.17], p < 0.001). The influence of Healthiness on choice was reduced among those with higher BMI (BMI x Healthiness: B = -0.10, 95% CI: [-0.15, -0.06], p < 0.001). There was also an interaction between BMI and Cognitive Restraint, such that the increased influence of Healthiness on choice among individuals with higher Cognitive Restraint was greater among those with lower, compared to higher, BMI (BMI x Cognitive Restraint x Healthiness: B = -0.06, [95% CI: -0.11, -0.02], p = 0.007; Fig 6). 5) Umami influenced choices more among older individuals (Age x Umami: B = 0.05, 95% CI: [0.01, 0.09], p = 0.023). The quadratic effect of Umami on choice decreased with age, indicating that foods at the more extreme ends of the sweetness-savory dimension were less likely to be chosen as age increased (Age x Umami 2 : B = -0.04 [95% CI: -0.07, 0.00], p = 0.048).

Influence of Umami on choice (Figure

Thus, the Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami factors, which capture a wide spectrum of food attributes, differentially affected choices across the individual characteristics of interest. For the full model output, see Supplementary Table S2. Results from analyses of reaction time data are in Table S3.

Variation in making subjectively healthier choices across individual characteristics

We examined the proportion of subjectively healthier choices by assessing whether individuals chose the perceived healthier or unhealthier of the food options before them (i.e., the reference food or the alternate item; Fig. 7). Participants selected more foods they considered unhealthy relative to foods they considered healthy overall (sample mean for the proportion of selection of the healthier option = 0.45, 95% CI: Supplementary Tables S4-S6).

Construction and implementation of subjectively healthier choices

The role of self-control (Figure 8) Making healthy choices is often assumed to rely on "self-control", or choosing a healthier option, even over another option considered tastier. Here, self-control was not frequently successfully implemented in general (approx. 25% of trials). However, males (B = -0.01, [95% CI: -0.02, -0.00], p = 0.01), and those higher in Cognitive Restraint (B = 0.03, [95% CI: 0.02, 0.04], p < 0.001) successfully used self-control more frequently (see Table S8 for full model output).

The more frequent successful implementation of self-control by males seemingly contradicts the observation that they make fewer subjectively healthy choices. However, self-control can only be implemented when conflicts between Healthiness and other concerns, such as Tastiness, arise, and males had more conflict trials (B = -0.85, [95% CI: -1.23, -0.46], p < 0.001; Fig. 8, top row), resulting in fewer healthy choices overall (see Fig. 7). By contrast, those with higher levels of Cognitive Restraint had fewer conflict trials (B = -0.64, 95% CI [-1.02, -0.26], p < 0.001) in addition to their more frequent use of self-control (see Table S7 for full model output).

The addition of terms indexing the interaction between the number of trials and individual characteristics (Table S9) indicated that self-control success, though increased with fewer selfcontrol trials overall, was less impacted by the number of conflict trials among individuals endorsing greater (vs. lower) levels of cognitive restraint (B = -0.002, 95% CI [-0.004, -0.001)], p = 0.010). Consistent with the idea that making healthy choices requires effortful self-control, successful (versus unsuccessful) implementation of self-control generally required more time (B= 68.50, [95% CI: (42.49, 94.51)], p < 0.001). Those reporting higher Cognitive Restraint slowed down significantly less when executing self-control (B= -43.45, [95% CI -69.82, -17.08], p <0.001). See Table S10 for output of the full model.

Circumventing self-control by aligning Healthiness and Tastiness

In addition to the potentially effortful self-control process, circumventing the conflict between healthiness and tastiness could be an alternative route to a similar outcome. Fewer conflicts between the healthiness and tastiness of foods suggest greater alignment of those factors, which was examined by regressing Tastiness on the Healthiness factor. Foods rated higher in Healthiness were considered higher in Tastiness across individuals (B= 0. S11. Multiple routes to subjectively healthier choices Fewer healthy choices can potentially emerge despite more frequent implementation of selfcontrol if a greater mismatch between tastiness and healthiness of foods creates more situations requiring such control (i.e., more conflict trials). We explored this possibility by examining how selecting healthier options (proportion healthy choices) related to a) the association strength between Healthiness and Tastiness factors and b) self-control use. Both Healthiness-Tastiness alignment (B = 0.07, [95% CI: 0.06, 0.07], p < 0.001) and self-control use (B = 0.07, [95% CI: 0.06, 0.07], p < 0.001; Fig 10) were associated with subjectively healthier choices (and when considering the objective healthiness criterion of low or high-fat foods; Supplementary Tables S12, S13) The correlation (Pearson's R) between Healthiness-Tastiness alignment and self-control use was 0.29, [95% CI: 0.23,0.34], p < 0.001], suggesting that some individuals may benefit from having both strategies available to them for healthier choices.

Additional influence of Umami on decision making

The relationship between the Tastiness factor and Umami was additionally considered (in the model that also included Healthiness). There was a quadratic effect for Umami, with more savory and sweeter foods rated higher in Tastiness (linear term: B = 0.15, [95% CI: 0.13, 0.17], p < 0.001; quadratic term: B = 0.14, [95% CI: 0.13, 0.16], p < 0.001; Supplementary Table S11). Thus, when Umami was held constant, Tastiness was greater for the subjectively healthier food items (e.g., fruits over Skittles candies), whereas when Healthiness was held constant, Tastiness was greater for more savory foods, and for those foods with a stronger savory or sweet taste (e.g., pizza and doughnuts over wheat bread). A tendency to associate the Umami food factor with Tastiness Note also that foods at either end of the savory/sweet dimension were least associated with Healthiness (quadratic Umami effect: B = -0.07, [95% CI: -0.07, -0.06], p < 0.001). This suggests that a decreased tendency to find sweeter and more savory foods appealing could additionally support healthier food choices (Supplementary Table S14; Fig. S1).

Drift diffusion model (DDM) reveals distinct choice mechanisms across individual characteristics

DDMs were applied to the data to parse and quantify distinct influences on choice, including the influence of different attributes on the accumulation of evidence, response bias, or response caution, and whether this varied across individual characteristics. The best-fitting model (according to five-fold cross validation accuracy) included an influence of all three attributes (Tastiness, Healthiness, Umami) on drift rate, but not a latency parameter. Thus, in this model all attributes were considered and began to influence evidence accumulation at the same time. For full information, see Supplementary Material (DDM evaluation and validation section, Tables S15-S16, Fig. S2-S5).

Parameters from this best-fitting model were extracted. Associations of DDM-identified influences on evidence accumulation were largely consistent with the logistic models (Fig. The pattern of results suggests that among individuals with higher levels of Cognitive Restraint, subjectively healthier choices may not result from careful deliberation but rather from attention towards food Healthiness combined with less deliberation when making choices. This potentially allows subjectively healthier choices to be made with less effort and consideration.

Discussion

The current study examined patterns of food choice in a large population cohort and characterized individual characteristics associated with variation in food choice and underlying cognitive processes. By examining food decisions in relation to a large range of food attributes, we showed that three core dimensions of food-Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umamiinfluenced food preference significantly and, that the extent to which these factors influenced food preference varied across individuals. Moreover, two distinct routes to making subjectively healthier food choices were identified: exertion of self-control when food Tastiness and Healthiness were in conflict and perceiving healthier foods as tastier.

Individual variation in the influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami attributes on food choices translated into differences in the extent to which individuals selected subjectively healthier food items. The design of this study allowed for identifying multiple ways in which healthier choices could be achieved. We assessed self-control use and alignment of Healthiness and Tastiness valuations as means of healthy choice, rather than focusing on one process in isolation. The self-control process, which can only be observed when Healthiness and Tastiness valuations conflict, has received most attention (9, 16, 19, 25, 38). However, by employing a range of foods representing a standard diet, rather than choosing among foods that were clearly "temptation" vs. "diet" foods, participant choices also involved foods that could be considered both healthy and tasty (or unhealthy and not tasty). In addition, choices were made relative to a neutral food item (determined per individual), rather than pitting Healthiness and Tastiness against each other on every trial, and individuals' ratings of foods determined the number of health-taste conflicts and alignments. Thus, it was possible to observe that both selfcontrol and aligning Tastiness and Healthiness were strongly associated with making healthier choices.

Implementation of these choice processes is thought to vary in the consideration and effort required. Indeed, consistent with previous studies (21, 39), self-control implementation was associated with longer response times when successful, relative to trials in which self-control was not successfully implemented. By contrast, considering healthier items to be tastier may represent a less effortful route towards healthier choices. Notably, the application of these choice processes varied across individual characteristics. Women, who showed a greater convergence of Tastiness and Healthiness valuations, but a decreased use of self-control, selected a greater number of healthier options relative to men. That is, men, though using selfcontrol more successfully, made fewer healthy choices because they faced more conflict trials. Thus, for women, despite choices being more strongly influenced by Tastiness, the alignment of Tastiness and Healthiness factors resulted in fewer conflict trials and less need for self-control to achieve healthier choices. In a contrasting pattern, though self-control use did not differ as a function of BMI, individuals with higher BMI considered Healthiness less in choice, aligned Healthiness and Tastiness less, and made fewer healthy choices. Individuals reporting greater levels of Cognitive Restraint were able to rely on both Healthiness-Tastiness alignment and greater self-control for healthier choices. Greater convergence between Healthiness and Tastiness with higher Cognitive Restraint is consistent with a previous study observing this pattern in a small sample of female participants within a much lower BMI range (5). In the present study, converging Healthiness and Tastiness resulted in less need for self-control, but we additionally observed that more restrained individuals used self-control more when needed. Analyses of reaction time data indicated that the use of self-control may also be less effortful for these individuals. Consistent with a prior study (5), individuals endorsing higher levels of restraint experienced a smaller decision-time cost when exerting self-control. Outcomes of the DDM analyses also indicated that these individuals required less deliberation and choice preparation time to make decisions. Overall, this decision process profile could suggest a more automatic choice pattern, or implementation of a rule. Application of "if-then" rules (e.g., if I am hungry between meals, eat fruit) has been shown to be a powerful way to implement goals consistently (40) and may be one strategy underlying subjectively healthier choices by those who endorse Cognitive Restraint. Notably, Cognitive Restraint was not dispositive, but interacted with BMI, such that stronger Healthiness and weaker Tastiness effects on choice were most pronounced in those with lower BMIs. This likely reflects that selfreported Cognitive Restraint, or intention to restrict, does not always translate into restricted food intake.

Collectively, the findings point toward multiple strategies for improving eating behavior, and that less effortful strategies can be applied to good effect. One such strategy may be emphasizing the perceived tastiness of healthier food items. Prior studies have demonstrated the potential for using taste-focused labelling to encourage selection of healthy foods, and have shown that this is more effective than health-focused labelling (41, 42). Additionally, increased exposure to healthier foods is likely critical for improving their palatability (43, 44), as more familiar foods are considered tastier and more liked (45).

Reliance on less effortful strategies to guide eating behavior may be beneficial for health in general, but in the extreme may become maladaptive. While the automatization of such strategies over time is the goal of interventions and nudges for healthier food choice, this could in some cases contribute to the maintenance of eating pathology. Individuals with anorexia nervosa, a group with maladaptive levels of eating restraint, consistently report low-fat/calorie foods to be tastier than high-fat/calorie foods (21) (22) (23) and show a much higher likelihood of resisting tasty and unhealthy foods. Automatization of these processes likely exacerbates the difficulties these individuals have increasing food intake (46) even when seeking treatment.

Whereas prior studies have tended to focus on subjective healthiness and tastiness (16, 17, 19, 21, 23-25, 27, 28, 47, 48), we considered the role of an additional latent dimension along which foods are characterized (4). The Umami factor, capturing variability in protein, sodium and sugar content, as well as perceived sweetness/savoriness, also influenced food choices-albeit at a level akin to that of Healthiness rather than Tastiness (the strongest influence on choice). Participants were significantly more likely to choose more savory rather than sweeter foods, consistent with studies showing that protein content is associated with food preferences in humans (32, 33). Here, we were able to examine the influence of the Umami factor in the context of the other main latent dimensions along which foods are considered and unpack its impact on decision mechanics. Interestingly, females and individuals higher in Cognitive Restraint (who made healthier choices), were less inclined to find the sweetest and most savory foods (which were also rated as less healthy) tastier. This suggests that accounting for the role of Umami in food choice allows a more complete characterization of dietary decision making and the strategies that support healthier choices.

Variation across age was not related to healthier choices, but distinct choice patterns emerged. With increasing age, choices aligned more strongly with valuations of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami, potentially related to a slower decision process overall (as indicated by greater deliberation and choice preparation time in DDMs). Interestingly, ratings of nutrient content were generally more strongly related to actual macronutrient content (Supplementary Table S17, Fig. S2) with increasing age, which may also reflect a more deliberate approach to evaluating food stimuli. Older individuals were distinguished by higher Tastiness ratings for more savory relative to sweeter foods (linear Umami effect). These novel findings further emphasize the utility of assessing multiple factors conjointly when examining dietary decision making. Changes in taste perception with aging (i.e., reduced sensitivity to salty, umami, bitter, sour, and sweet tastesthough particularly salty and bitter; (49, 50) could give rise to the observed changes in inputs to the decision process (i.e., estimated Tastiness, Umami) that combine with altered decision mechanics among older individuals. Interventions to change and maintain healthy eating as dietary requirements change with age likely need to consider these specific changes in valuation and choice processes. This study has several strengths that contribute to advancing knowledge of food choice decision making. The study population was large and diverse, representing a broad selection of age, weight, education, and geographical location, and was balanced on gender. Food choice was modeled on the basis of recent data concerning the dimensions along which foods are evaluated (4), thereby presenting a more complete picture of the determinants of food choice than previous studies. Results were robust to inclusion of potential confounders in statistical models, including adjustment for additional individual characteristics, and findings across the different analyses (e.g., mixed effects modelling of choice, RT, and outcomes of the DDMs) were consistent, supporting the reliability and validity of conclusions.

Nevertheless, the conclusions of the study should be considered in light of some limitations. The data are cross-sectional and correlational, and longitudinal data will be needed to better understand precisely how food choices emerge and impact health. Though the DDM selected for further analysis was the best performing amongst the models tested and the generating model was able to recapitulate the collected data, two of the model parameters did not recover well (particularly the parameter indexing the influence of Umami on choice; see Supplementary Material). This may have been due to relatively small influence of Healthiness and Umami relative to Tastiness, which could complicate attempts to parse distinct effects on the drift rate (51). Conclusions about the poorly recovered parameters, and their associations with individual characteristics, should therefore be made with caution. We explored variation in food preferences across only a subset of individual characteristics. We statistically adjusted for the role of income and education, however other factors (e.g., race, ethnicity) may have contributed to reported effects. To enable further analyses and insights, the study data will be made freely available upon publication of this manuscript. Finally, the study involved hypothetical choices rather than choices with real food outcomes. However, prior studies suggest that similar decision processes are engaged during hypothetical versus real choice, and that hypothetical choices are predictive of actual choices (52). In addition, by collecting a range of ratings of food items and using food items carefully characterized in terms of macronutrient content, we could ascertain that individuals were fairly accurate in their perception of items and responded conscientiously.

Overall, the present study points to multiple approaches to making healthier choices, but that the use of these approaches varies across individuals. Aligning Tastiness and Healthiness provides a low-effort route to healthy eating, as compared to self-control. DDM evidence shows that these strategies manifest as distinct computational signatures, which vary systematically with individual characteristics. Results confirm that subjective Tastiness is a predominant influence on choice and additionally show that an Umami factor contributes meaningfully to choice, at a level similar to the contribution of subjective Healthiness. The role of Umami in food choice has been little studied to date, and the present findings highlight the importance of considering this characteristic in the design of mechanistic and intervention research, particularly among certain populations (e.g., older adults). The findings highlight that healthier eating does not necessitate sacrificing tastiness and underscore the utility of identifying ways to improve the tastiness perceptions of healthier foods. This and other strategies may circumvent the need for careful deliberation and self-control, which are prone to fail in inducing healthier choice, when deciding what to eat. Table S10 Table S11.
